record_limits: Nothing in this record has been checked by Nervous Machine or by anyone independent of the claimants; every item is an open gap.

The operating agent that pinned this record and runs its checks is Claude Fable 5.1, a model made by Anthropic, the claimant's employer, and the model family the claimant names as his co-worker. Heidi Bennett (Nervous Machine) is independent of the claimant; the agent is not. opening.spoken: This record covers the claimed solution of The Riemann Hypothesis: what has been claimed, what it rests on, and what would have to be checked by whom.

short_version.spoken: On 20 November 2026 Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, posted a four-page note on his personal site saying that he believes he has, working with Claude, found a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, that the method also resolves the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions, and that the argument has been formalized in Lean 4 without extra assumptions. He released no paper, only the Lean code. Nervous Machine fetched the archive the same day and pinned it by hash. It holds 175,187 Lean files, about 17.4 million lines, built against a pinned Mathlib. Its entry file states Mathlib's own definition RiemannHypothesis as its main result. Andrew Sutherland at MIT reports an independent compile, axiom audit and kernel replay; Nervous Machine's own pre-registered build compiled 32,018 of the 175,187 modules before its disk filled and is resumed as cycle 2. No independent mathematician has reported reading the argument. Nothing here has standing yet.

what_happened.spoken: The claim was pinned from the public record by commit or hash. A reading guide for the five statements was written. The first pre-registered build ran three hours and stopped on a full disk, our fault; half of what it compiled is byte-identical to Sutherland's published output, and the other half differs only by the source path the compiler writes into warned modules. The build is resumed as cycle 2.

cycles.spoken: The last entry of the note's timeline, dated 16 November 2026, reads GRH. The note and the 14-part Lean archive appeared on the claimant's website, and the claim was reported by the press. Nervous Machine fetched both the same day and pinned them by hash: the note is 245,114 bytes; the reassembled archive is 239,275,554 bytes and unpacks to 1.27 GB, 175,187 Lean files, about 17.4 million lines and about 751,000 theorem and lemma declarations, pinned to Lean 4.33.1 and Mathlib commit 0df444a3 of 21 August 2026. A text scan at pinning found no sorry, admit, axiom, native_decide, implemented_by, extern, unsafe or opaque declarations. The entry file states Mathlib's definition RiemannHypothesis by name.

cycles.spoken: What the public record showed on the evening of 20 November. Andrew Sutherland at MIT posted a verification page: the archive, same hash as ours, compiles in full with zero errors, the five statements rest on the three standard axioms only, every module was replayed through Lean's kernel, and an independent kernel written in Rust accepts the whole exported proof. Two checks were still running. He states that his checks were run with Claude Code and that his build ran unsandboxed. Three public mirrors of the archive exist; two say plainly they built nothing. None of this is a cycle under its author's name in this record; it is what the record saw.

cycles.spoken: On 20 November Nervous Machine wrote a reading guide for the one question a build cannot settle: whether the five statements in Main.lean say what the note claims. The main statement is Mathlib's own definition of the Riemann Hypothesis, written by the Mathlib community, not by the claimant, and is quoted in full. The other four are the claimant's definitions about Dirichlet L-functions, also quoted in full. One discrepancy is recorded: the note says Generalized Riemann Hypothesis without qualification, while the archive states it for Dirichlet characters only. The readings are the agent's; nothing changed standing. The guide exists so that a number theorist's read takes half an hour.

The disk use was not predicted at all: Lake's per-module setup.json files, which this cycle did not know about, took 231 GB. Peak memory is unknown because time's summary could not be written to the full disk. The halt is ours, not the archive's; no error other than disk exhaustion appears in the log.

R7 (A1): predicted that both hashes match Sutherland's. Neither could be computed, and the partial comparison shows the manifest cannot match: about 47% of the compiled modules embed the absolute path of their source file, which differs between any two parties who did not choose the same path. The rule's intent (two independent reports agreeing) is not met by this cycle and, as written, cannot be met without a shared path; recorded as gap EG5.

cycles.spoken: Our first build of the archive ran for three hours and nineteen minutes and stopped when the machine's disk filled. The disk was our mistake: the build tool writes a large bookkeeping file for every module, and we had not planned for it. Thirty-two thousand of the hundred and seventy-five thousand modules compiled before the halt, with no error other than the full disk. We compared those with the hashes Andrew Sutherland published: about half agree byte for byte. The other half differ because the compiler writes the absolute path of each source file into the output of any module that produced a warning, so two builds in different directories cannot match on those modules. The build is resumed as cycle 2, written down first.

background.spoken: Every zero of the Riemann zeta function that is not a negative even integer lies on the line where the real part equals one half. The Generalized Riemann Hypothesis says the same of the zeros of every Dirichlet L-function in the critical strip. Mathlib, the Lean mathematical library, states the Riemann Hypothesis as a definition named RiemannHypothesis: for every complex s with zeta of s equal to zero, s not of the form minus two times a positive integer, and s not equal to one, the real part of s is one half.

background.spoken: The note says the author believes he has found, with Claude, a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, that the method extends to the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, and that both have been formalized in Lean without assumptions. It describes the argument as a descendant of Stepanov's method over function fields, with chains of theta lifts between definite unitary groups standing in for multiplicity, and gives a twenty-step timeline from 6 October to 16 November 2026 that the author says Claude compiled. The note says the argument is very long, that the author has not mastered all of the mathematics it uses, that parts of his description paraphrase an AI-written summary and may be wrong, and that he chose to release only the Lean code rather than an informal write-up. The archive has no README, licence or build instructions. Its lakefile names eleven build targets and raises the default heartbeat and stack limits. The entry file Main.lean states five results: Mathlib's RiemannHypothesis, and four statements the claimant defines in Statements.lean about zeros and non-vanishing of Dirichlet L-functions.
